claims.text: The initial nanoparticles are sub-10 nm equiatomic Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt particles.
The initial nanoparticles are a single-phase solid solution or a metastable mixed state.
The particles are heated in vacuum from 300 K to 1000 K.
The sluggish-diffusion assumption breaks down above 600 K in this nanoparticle system.
A high surface-to-volume ratio lowers the activation barriers for surface diffusion.
Above 600 K, surface diffusion has a significantly lower activation energy than bulk diffusion.
Surface-energy minimization overrides bulk sluggish-diffusion effects and drives rapid segregation at the nanoscale.
Elevated-temperature treatment can produce element-specific near-surface enrichment and depletion in a high-entropy alloy.
Au and Pt segregate to surfaces or interfaces, while Co and Ni segregate inward or form distinct phases.
The system undergoes rapid phase separation rather than remaining thermodynamically stabilized as a homogeneous alloy.
High curvature raises the chemical potential of the smallest particles.
Ostwald ripening, evaporation, vaporization, or coalescence causes the smallest particles to disappear.
Nanoparticles smaller than 5 nm will be rapidly lost during heating.
Remaining particles will develop significant shape anisotropy or faceting because of surface segregation.
At 1000 K, the particles will contain phase-separated domains rather than a stable homogeneous single phase.
Surface effects dominate structural evolution specifically for particles smaller than 10 nm.
For particles larger than 50 nm, bulk diffusion kinetics and entropy stabilization become more significant.
Prior models predict thermal stability from sluggish diffusion and high configurational entropy in equiatomic high-entropy nanoparticles.
In-situ HRTEM and EDS during heating can test particle-size evolution, morphology, phase separation, and element-resolved surface composition.
Diffusion coefficients can be derived from measured particle-coalescence rates.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis places breakdown above 600 K, but the support rule treats phase separation and particle loss at any temperature below 800 K as supportive, including temperatures below the stated 600 K threshold.
